title: Ride-share legalisation (2015 to 2018): re-evaluation with saturated effects
design: Staggered: each group of states that legalised in the same year against states that had not yet, with class x year and state x year effects.
comparison: ACT/NSW from 2016 against VIC/NT/WA; SA/QLD/TAS from 2017 against VIC/NT/WA; VIC/NT from 2018 against WA
grade_reason: a pre-reform year of the primary outcome lies outside its 95% placebo band
headline: Not identified: business entry rate −2.2 per 100 businesses a year (p = 0.17), saturated fixed effects.

category_summaries.competition: Business entry rate: −2.2 per 100 businesses a year (p = 0.17; detectable from 4.3). Business exit rate: −0.3 per 100 businesses a year (p = 0.59; detectable from 2.2).
category_summaries.prices: Urban transport fares: prices relative to the CPI: −0.3% (log points) (p = 0.85; detectable from 5.0).

key_insights: The question: did legalising ride-sharing (2015 to 2018) change how many taxi and ride businesses started or closed, or fares?
The comparison: Staggered: each group of states that legalised in the same year against states that had not yet, with class x year and state x year effects.

What we found: the effect cannot be identified: a pre-reform year of the primary outcome lies outside its 95% placebo band, so the treated group was already moving apart before the reform. The registered layer's estimate (−2.2 per 100 businesses a year) is not an effect.
Other outcomes: business exit rate −0.3 (p = 0.59); urban transport fares: prices relative to the CPI −0.3 (p = 0.85).
How precise: only changes larger than about 4.3 per 100 businesses a year could have been detected.

Robustness (not pre-registered): across 11 variants (each state left out, other windows and pre-periods, weights and data vintages) the business entry rate estimate keeps its sign in 9, reaches p < 0.05 in 1, and ranges from −4.5 to +2.8.

Compared with the earlier evaluation (2026-10-15, now archived): it found that the effect could not be identified (business entry rate +0.2 per 100 businesses a year). The conclusion is unchanged; the smallest detectable effect is now 4.3, down from 6.0. This evaluation uses the estimator chosen in the blinded power study and the latest data.
What it means: these data cannot separate the reform from what was already happening.

method.summary: Saturated fixed effects on ANZSIC classes by state and financial year, the layer chosen for this reform in the blinded power study, with every other layer reported side by side.

equations.label: Saturated fixed effects
equations.text: y_{cst} = α_{cs} + δ_{ct} + γ_{st} + β·D_{cst} + ε_{cst}

equations.label: Year by year
equations.text: y_{cst} = α_{cs} + δ_{ct} + γ_{st} + Σ_{k≠−1} β_{k}·1[t − T_{s} = k]·T_{cs} + ε_{cst}

terms.meaning: Entries (or exits) per 100 businesses operating at the start of year t, class c, state s
1 for the reform's class in a treated state (or city) from its first exposed period to the end of its window
a level for each class in each state
each class's national movement in each period (industry cycles, product-wide price swings)
each state's movement in each period (state booms and slumps)

method.estimand: The average change in the outcome for the reform's classes in treated states over the window, beyond the same classes elsewhere and the treated states' other classes, net of the mean placebo estimate.
method.identification: Without the reform, the treated classes in treated states would have moved like the same classes elsewhere plus their states' other classes (parallel trends in the saturated model; for synthetic DiD, like the weighted comparison cells).
method.inference: The same estimator applied to up to 40 placebo industry groups (or CPI classes) at the reform's states and dates gives the no-effect distribution: the p-value is the share of centred placebo estimates at least as large; the 90% interval subtracts their 5th and 95th percentiles. Benjamini-Hochberg q-values across the specification's primary outcomes. Placebo states and fake dates check the reform's own classes.
steps: Registered the layer, outcomes, windows and placebo pools in the specification before any treated post-reform outcome was computed.
Design stage: hid treated cells from first exposure, computed every layer's placebo distribution, the own-class placebos and the pre-reform event-study check.
Committed the design and plan, ran a blinded dry run, then one registered run with treated cells restored.
Judged the registered layer's estimate against its placebo distribution; reported every other layer side by side.

Confounder scan (not pre-registered; docs/confounder_scan.md): no other register change of high or medium relevance. Timing: the treated series moved most away from the reform period in: urban transport fares: prices relative to the CPI, ACT, 2015-Q1 (+3.5 × the usual step); urban transport fares: prices relative to the CPI, NSW, 2015-Q1 (+3.8 × the usual step); urban transport fares: prices relative to the CPI, QLD, 2017-Q1 (−5.0 × the usual step).
Re-evaluation: the earlier results were known when this specification was written; the estimator layers were fixed beforehand by the blinded power study.

tables.title: Ride-share legalisation (2015 to 2018): re-evaluation with saturated effects

panels.title: Panel A. Business entry rate, per 100 businesses a year (primary outcome; 7 treated cells)
Panel B. Business exit rate, per 100 businesses a year (secondary outcome; 7 treated cells)
Panel C. Urban transport fares: prices relative to the CPI, 100 × log points (secondary outcome; 7 treated cells)

notes: Panels A and B: entries and exits per 100 businesses operating at the start of the financial year, ANZSIC class × state, weighted by those businesses; 2007-08 to 2017-18 (11 periods), 431 classes, 8 states.
Panel C: 100 × log of the CPI class relative to All groups, CPI class × capital city × quarter, unweighted; 2005-Q1 to 2018-Q4 (56 periods), 87 classes, 8 cities.

Each column applies one estimator to the same panel. β is the average effect on the reform's classes in treated states (cities) over the window, net of the mean of the same estimator across the placebo groups. Columns (6) and (7) compare the treated group's average with reweighted untreated cells over each cohort's window; their observations and units are summed over cohorts.

The placebo standard deviation is the spread of the same estimator across up to 40 placebo industry groups (or CPI classes) given the reform's states and dates: the randomization-inference analogue of a standard error. p-values rank the estimate among the centred placebo estimates; with 40 placebos the smallest attainable is about 0.024, so *** cannot occur. Clustered standard errors are not reported: with seven or eight states they are unreliable, and the registered inference uses placebos.

MDE: the smallest effect detectable with 80% power at the 5% level (2.8 × the placebo standard deviation). Placebo groups: placebo industry groups (business outcomes) or CPI classes (prices). Pre-trend test: every event-study coefficient with k ≤ −2 (saturated model, net of the placebo mean) lies inside its 95% placebo band; a failure means the outcome is not identified. BH q-value: Benjamini–Hochberg across the specification's primary outcomes.
Source: alicia/analyses/phase5/reevaluations/estimate.json (registered run, 18 October 2026) and table_stats.json (samples, re-fitted to check every estimate reproduces).

tables.title: Ride-share legalisation (2015 to 2018): re-evaluation with saturated effects: robustness (not pre-registered)

panels.title: Panel B. Leave one state out

notes: Not pre-registered: written after the registered results were seen. It can show that a result is fragile; it cannot turn a variant into a finding.

Each row re-runs the registered estimator on a variant of the registered panel and judges it against its own no-effect distribution: the same placebo groups (or CPI classes), re-estimated on the variant with treated cells hidden, as at the design stage. Leave one state out drops a treated or comparison state. Window: the first exposed year (four quarters for prices) or the last year dropped. Pre-period: from four years (business counts) or five years (prices) before the first exposure. Unweighted: every cell counts equally. Other CABEE vintages: each year taken from the mean of the releases in which it is not final.

Pre-trend breakdown M̄: how large a post-reform departure from parallel trends, relative to the largest pre-reform change in the saturated event study, would be needed for the average post-reform effect to include zero (Rambachan and Roth relative magnitudes; approximate inference). Below 1, a departure no larger than one already seen before the reform could explain the estimate. The identified set at M̄ = 1 is the range of effects consistent with such a departure.

Own-industry placebo p: the registered estimate ranked among the reform's own industries in states that never adopted it at fake dates. Synthetic DiD pre-fit ratio: the spread of the treated-minus-weighted-controls gap before the reform, over the spread of the treated series; with few pre-reform periods a close fit is easy, so it shows little. Effective controls: 1 / Σ ω².
